question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity Vector at a Point in Time Given the Acceleration Vector
question.problem:
The acceleration $a$ at time $t$ of a particle $P$ moving in the $xy$-plane is given by

$$
a(t)=⟨1-3{t}^{2},4t-1⟩.
$$

Given that the particle has velocity $v=⟨-1,1⟩$ when $t=2,$ calculate the velocity vector of $P$ at time $t=1.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the velocity vector, we need to integrate the acceleration vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int ⟨1-3{t}^{2},4t-1⟩\text{d}t \\  & =⟨\int (1-3{t}^{2})\,\text{d}t,\int (4t-1)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨t-{t}^{3}+{C}_{1},2{t}^{2}-t+{C}_{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can solve for the constants of integration using the fact that $v(2)=⟨-1,1⟩.$ Substituting $t=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =⟨2-{2}^{3}+{C}_{1},2({2}^{2})-2+{C}_{2}⟩ \\ ⟨-1,1⟩ & =⟨-6+{C}_{1},6+{C}_{2}⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

so we must have ${C}_{1}=5$ and ${C}_{2}=-5.$ Therefore, the velocity is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =⟨t-{t}^{3}+5,2{t}^{2}-t-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity at time $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}v(1) & =⟨1-{1}^{3}+5,2({1}^{2})-1-5⟩ \\  & =⟨5,-4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus by Interchanging the Limits of Integration
question.problem: Let $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)-x.$ Find ${g}^{′}(2)$ given the function is defined by $g(x)={\int }_{x}^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t.$
question.worked_solution:
In this example, the variable limit $x$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of definite integrals, we can write

$$
g(x)={\int }_{x}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t=-{\int }_{0}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{x}^{0}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-{\int }_{0}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\int }_{0}^{x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi t)-t)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)-x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the value of ${g}^{′}(2),$ we substitute $x=2$ in the above:

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(2) & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi \cdot 2)-2) \\  & =-(0-2) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Using the Chain Rule
question.worked_solution:
To compute ${f}^{′}(x),$ we first make the substitution $u=3x-5$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{\int }_{3x-5}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of the definite integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{u}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}(-{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}u}{\int }_{1}^{u}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t-1)\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2u-1)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3x-5)\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2u-1)) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2(3x-5)-1) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x-11).\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Normal Random Variable on an Unbounded Interval
question.worked_solution:
Given a normal random variable $X∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(X<x)=P(Z<\frac{x-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =-2$ and $\sigma =3.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<-4.28) & =P(Z<\frac{-4.28-(-2)}{3}) \\  & =P(Z<-0.76) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.76) \\  & =Φ(-0.76)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070250/assets/56f9956d27f7527106869001273833c863d26053baf8c624c98d4ec2fb3c7f7b.png)

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(-0.76)=0.2236.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(X<-4.28)=0.2236.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing the Probability of a Normal Random Variable on a Bounded Interval
question.problem:
The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. Given that $X∼N(4,{6}^{2}),$ compute $P(-3.2
$z$$\,0.00\,$$\,0.01\,$$\,0.02\,$
$\,-1.3\,$ $\,0.0968\,$ $\,0.0951\,$ $\,0.0934\,$
$\,-1.2\,$ $\,0.1151\,$ $\,0.1131\,$ $\,0.1112\,$
$\,-1.1\,$ $\,0.1357\,$ $\,0.1335\,$ $\,0.1314\,$
$z$$\,0.07\,$$\,0.08\,$$\,0.09\,$
$\,-0.3\,$ $\,0.3557\,$ $\,0.3520\,$ $\,0.3483\,$
$\,-0.2\,$ $\,0.3936\,$ $\,0.3897\,$ $\,0.3859\,$
$\,-0.1\,$ $\,0.4325\,$ $\,0.4286\,$ $\,0.4247\,$
question.worked_solution:
Given a normal random variable $X∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),$ we have

$$
P(a<X<b)=P(\frac{a-\mu }{\sigma }<Z<\frac{b-\mu }{\sigma })
$$

where $Z∼N(0,1)$ is a standard normal random variable. In our case, we have $\mu =4$ and $\sigma =6.$

First, we transform $X$ into a standard normal random variable $Z$ by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-3.2<X<2.86) & =P(\frac{-3.2-4}{6}<Z<\frac{2.86-4}{6}) \\  & =P(-1.2<Z<-0.19)\end{aligned}
$$

The required probability is represented by the area shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070250/assets/1ed2c43f507a4d0ddd54126bcd3efaa2fa9b56c63ea908e8567e6959e3fc67bc.png)

Now, we express the required probability in terms of $Φ(z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.2<Z<-0.19) & =P(Z<-0.19)-P(Z\le -1.2) \\  & =P(Z\le -0.19)-P(Z\le -1.2) \\  & =Φ(-0.19)-Φ(-1.2)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1.2) & =0.1151 \\ Φ(-0.19) & =0.4247\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(-1.2<Z<-0.19) & =Φ(-0.19)-Φ(-1.2) \\  & =0.4247-0.1151 \\  & =0.3096.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that

$$
P(-3.2<X<2.86)=0.3096.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Using a Percentage Points Table and Symmetry To Find the Z-Score for a Given Probability
question.problem:
The table below gives the values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p,$ where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. Find the value of $z$ such that $P(Z>z)=0.30.$

| $\,p\,$ | $0.55$ | $0.60$ | $0.65$ | $0.70$ | $0.75$ | $0.80$ | $0.85$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.1257\,$ | $\,0.2533\,$ | $\,0.3853\,$ | $\,0.5244\,$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
First, we express the given information in terms of $Φ,$ using the complement:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>z) & =0.30 \\ 1-P(Z\le z) & =0.30 \\ 1-Φ(z) & =0.30 \\ Φ(z) & =1-0.30 \\ Φ(z) & =0.70\end{aligned}
$$

So, we are looking for the value of $z$ such that

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.70).
$$

We look for the column in the table that corresponds to $p=0.70,$ and we find that

$$
p=0.70\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(p)=0.5244.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
z={Φ}^{-1}(0.70)=0.5244.
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Missing Parameter Using Symmetry When the Mean Is Nonzero
question.problem:
The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. Given that $X∼N(\mu ,{15}^{2})$ is a normal random variable with $P(-5\mu <X<7\mu )=0.5762,$ determine $\mu .$

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7580\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8159\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ |

*Hint: Note that the interval $-5\mu <X<7\mu $ is symmetric about the mean $\mu .$*
question.worked_solution:
Note that we can write the given probability as

$$
P(\mu -6\mu <X<\mu +6\mu )=0.5762,
$$

which tells us that the interval $-5\mu <X<7\mu $ is symmetric about the mean $\mu .$

First, we find the cumulative probability using symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\mu -6\mu <X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.5762 \\ 2P(\mu <X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.5762 \\ P(\mu <X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.2881 \\ P(X<\mu +6\mu )-P(X<\mu ) & =0.2881 \\ P(X<\mu +6\mu )-0.5 & =0.2881 \\ P(X<\mu +6\mu ) & =0.7881 \\ P(X\le \mu +6\mu ) & =0.7881 \\ P(X\le 7\mu ) & =0.7881\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 7\mu ) & =0.7881 \\ P(Z\le \frac{7\mu -\mu }{15}) & =0.7881 \\ Φ(\frac{6\mu }{15}) & =0.7881 \\ \frac{6\mu }{15} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.7881) \\ \frac{2\mu }{5} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.7881)\end{aligned}
$$

 

According to the table, we have

$$
Φ(0.8)=0.7881\,⇒\,{Φ}^{-1}(0.7881)=0.8.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2\mu }{5} & =0.8 \\ 2\mu  & =4 \\ \mu  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Probability Given a Normal Distribution Model
question.problem:
In a factory, the amount of sugar on a cookie is normally distributed with a mean of $15$ grams and a standard deviation of $0.8$ grams. What is the probability that the amount of sugar on a randomly selected cookie is less than $14$ grams? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.2\,$ | $\,0.1093\,$ | $\,0.1075\,$ | $\,0.1056\,$ |
| $\,-1.1\,$ | $\,0.1292\,$ | $\,0.1271\,$ | $\,0.1251\,$ |
| $\,-1.0\,$ | $\,0.1515\,$ | $\,0.1492\,$ | $\,0.1469\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the amount of sugar (in grams) on the cookies. Then we have $X∼N(15,{0.8}^{2}).$

We want to find $P(X<14).$ First, we write this as a cumulative probability:

$$
P(X<14)=P(X\le 14)
$$

Then, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 14) & =P(Z\le \frac{14-15}{0.8}) \\  & =P(Z\le -1.25) \\  & =Φ(-1.25)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(-1.25)=0.1056≈0.11.
$$

Therefore, the probability that the amount of sugar on a randomly selected cookie is less than $14$ grams is approximately $0.11.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding an Unknown Population Parameter Using a Percentage Points Table
question.problem:
A cinema admission fee is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ dollars and a standard deviation of $$0.7.$ In addition, in $94%$ of cases the admission fee is between $$0.75\mu $ and $$1.25\mu .$ Find the average cinema admission fee, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $p$ | $\,0.75\,$ | $\,0.80\,$ | $\,0.85\,$ | $\,0.90\,$ | $\,0.95\,$ | $\,0.97\,$ | $\,0.99\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,0.6745\,$ | $\,0.8416\,$ | $\,1.0364\,$ | $\,1.2816\,$ | $\,1.6449\,$ | $\,1.8808\,$ | $\,2.3263\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent an admission fee. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{0.7}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(0.75\mu <X<1.25\mu )=0.94.$ First, we convert this to a cumulative probability:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0.75\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.94 \\ 2P(\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.94 \\ P(\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.47 \\ P(X<\mu )+P(\mu <X<1.25\mu ) & =0.5+0.47 \\ P(X<1.25\mu ) & =0.97\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we convert $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.25\mu ) & =0.97 \\ P(Z<\frac{0.25\mu }{0.7}) & =0.97 \\ Φ(\frac{0.25\mu }{0.7}) & =0.97 \\ \frac{0.25\mu }{0.7} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.97)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.97)≈1.8808.
$$

Finally then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{0.25\mu }{0.7} & =1.8808 \\ 0.25\mu  & =1.31656 \\ \mu  & =\frac{1.31656}{0.25} \\  & ≈5.27.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding an Unknown Population Parameter Using a Percentage Points Table
question.problem:
The lifetime of a lithium-ion battery produced by a particular company is normally distributed with a mean of $\mu $ years and a standard deviation of $0.5$ years.
Additionally, $3%$ of batteries last less than $1.75$ years. Find the mean $\mu $, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.10\,$ | $\,0.15\,$ | $\,0.20\,$ | $\,0.25\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |
question.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the lifetime of a randomly selected battery. Then we have $X∼N(\mu ,{0.5}^{2}),$ and we want to find the mean $\mu .$ 

We know that $P(X<1.75)=0.03.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<1.75) & =0.03 \\ P(Z\le \frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5}) & =0.03 \\ Φ(\frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5}) & =0.03 \\ \frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5} & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.03).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.03)=-1.8808.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1.75-\mu }{0.5} & =-1.8808 \\ 1.75-\mu  & =-0.9404 \\ \mu  & ≈2.69.\end{aligned}
$$
